architecture.mechanism: The paper identifies clearance between the flat-faced follower and its guides as a source of impact and friction during follower motion, and shows that non-linear dynamic analysis (validated against experiment via the largest Lyapunov exponent) can quantify how this clearance-driven impact and friction governs follower motion — i.e., excessive guide clearance converts steady cam-driven displacement into impact-loaded, non-linear follower behavior that raises cyclic contact stress on the follower face, promoting surface fatigue spalling.
architecture.intervention: Because the cam profile, 16 mm follower diameter, and 420 cycles/min are fixed, intervene on the guide-to-follower-stud clearance instead: build the paper's non-linear dynamic model of the folding-station cam-follower linkage (including clearance, impact, and friction), use it to identify the clearance value that minimizes impact severity, and re-specify the follower studs with close-fitting guide bushings/sleeves to hold that reduced clearance — with the certified cam geometry and follower diameter unchanged and no added maintenance beyond the weekly window.
architecture.expected_effect: Lower impact and friction forces at the cam-follower interface reduce cyclic Hertzian contact stress on the 16 mm flat-faced follower, extending surface fatigue life well beyond the current 6–9 weeks and cutting the metal debris that contaminates the food-contact zone.
architecture.falsification_test: Replicate the paper's optical-marker method on the running line: mount a high-resolution optical marker on a follower stem to capture y-direction motion at 420 cycles/min, extract the largest Lyapunov exponent and impact severity for the current clearance, then repeat with progressively reduced guide clearance; if reducing clearance does not measurably decrease impact severity/Lyapunov exponent and does not extend follower spalling life in a side-by-side trial, the mechanism is falsified.
